offence_severity: Life imprisonment with fine of Rs.1,000/-
physical_harm: Victim died instantly due to gunshot injuries to the brain and left eye, with nine other injuries on the body
key_evidence_accepted: The consistent and clear account of the incident given by the eye witnesses PW-2, PW-3 and PW-13, along with the medical evidence and FSL report, were accepted as credible and trustworthy by the Supreme Court.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible and trustworthy, noting that minor contradictions in their testimony do not affect the core of the prosecution case and are due to normal errors of observation.
bail_history: Bail bonds of the accused Balvir Singh and Bhav Singh shall stand discharged.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 11.03.1998; Trial judgment: 26.08.2008; High Court decision: 26.08.2008; Supreme Court decision: 2019
legal_representation: Raj Kishor Choudhary , Abdul Karim Ansari, Shakeel Ahmed, Ms. Chitranjali Negi, Aftab Ali Khan, Sanjay Jain, Advs. for the Appellant; Mrs. Swarupama Chaturvedi, B. N. Dubey , Mukesh Kumar , Ms. Indira Bhakar , Ms. Aparna Trivedi, Santanu Singh, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed against the accused for the offences punishable under Sections 147, 148, 149, 341, 294, 323, 506B, 302 IPC and under Section 25 read with Section 27 of the Arms Act and under Section 3(2)(V) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act in the court of Special Judge, Sagar, M.P.
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction affirmed; High Court: Conviction affirmed; Supreme Court: Conviction of accused Nos. 2 and 3 under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC is set aside; Conviction of accused No.1 under Sections 302 IPC, 341 IPC and Section 25(1A) read with Section 27 of the Arms Act is affirmed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the eye witnesses PW-2, PW-3, and PW-13 provided a consistent and clear account of the incident, including specific overt acts by each accused. The medical evidence was not considered to undermine the eye witnesses' testimony, and the recovered pistol and FSL report supported the prosecution's case.
defence_argument: The appellants contended that the occurrence was a blind murder and that the eye witnesses' testimony suffered from material contradictions and inconsistencies. They also argued that the medical evidence contradicted the eye witnesses' accounts and that the prosecution failed to prove the common intention of the accused Nos. 2 and 3.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that minor discrepancies in the testimony of eye witnesses do not affect the trustworthiness of their accounts, especially when their evidence is corroborated by other evidence. It also emphasized that common intention under Section 34 IPC must be established through overt acts and shared criminal intent.
precedent_relied_upon: Appabhai and Another v. State of Gujarat (1988) Suppl. SCC 241; Annar eddy Sambasiva Reddy and Others v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2009) 12 SCC 546; Ramanand Yadav v. Prabhu Nath Jha and Others (2003) 12 SCC 606; Ramesh Singh alias Phooti v. State of A.P. (2004) 11 SCC 305; Dhanna v. State of M.P. (1996) 10 SCC 79
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed on accused No.1 (Harnam Singh) for his direct involvement in the murder, including the use of a country-made pistol, and for the aggravating circumstances of the victim's death.
judicial_aggravating_factors: The court considered the aggravating factors such as the victim's death, the use of a weapon, and the premeditated nature of the attack.
other_sentence_order: Accused No.1 (Harnam Singh) was to surrender himself within four weeks from the date of the judgment to serve the remaining sentence, failing which, he would be taken into custody. Accused Nos.2 and 3 were acquitted and their bail bonds were discharged.
